title: Sum Game
summary: Alice and Bob play a game where they take turns replacing '?' in a string num with any digit from '0' to '9'.
statement: Alice and Bob play a game where they take turns replacing '?' in a string num with any digit from '0' to '9'. Alice starts the game. The game continues until all '?' in num are replaced. Bob wins if the sum of the digits in the first half of num equals the sum of the digits in the second half. Alice wins if the sums are not equal. Assuming both players play optimally, determine the winner of the game.
constraints: num has even length up to 100000 and contains digits or '?'.
Alice and Bob alternately replace one question mark with any digit; Alice moves first.
Alice wins when final half sums differ, while Bob wins when they are equal; both optimize their result.
reference_solution:
def alice_wins_sum_game(num):
    half = len(num) // 2
    left_unknown = num[:half].count("?")
    right_unknown = num[half:].count("?")
    left_sum = sum(int(char) for char in num[:half] if char != "?")
    right_sum = sum(int(char) for char in num[half:] if char != "?")
    if (left_unknown + right_unknown) % 2 == 1:
        return True
    return left_sum - right_sum != 9 * (right_unknown - left_unknown) // 2
hints: Count question marks and fixed digit sums separately in the two halves.
An odd total number of moves gives Alice one unmatched choice, so she can force a difference.
With an even count, Bob can balance exactly only when the fixed difference equals 9/2 times the question-count imbalance.
Pairing Alice and Bob's optimal digit choices contributes nine per move pair, yielding the balance equation and its negation as Alice's winning test.

tests.explanation: There are no choices and both halves sum to seven, so Bob wins and the result is false.
Alice can force unequal half sums regardless of Bob's reply, so the result is true.
